SIRT1 expression sensitized ALL to panobinostat through activating mitochondrial activity and the mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway. Visual Abstract Abstract Epigenetic alterations, including histone acetylation, contribute to the malignant transformation of hematopoietic cells and disease progression, as well as the emergence of chemotherapy resistance. Targeting histone acetylation provides new strategies for the treatment of cancers. As a pan-histone deacetylase inhibitor, panobinostat has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of multiple myeloma and has shown promising antileukemia effects in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). However, the underlying drug resistance mechanism in ALL remains largely unknown. Using genome-wide Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas)9 (CRISPR/Cas9) screening, we identified mitochondrial activity as the driver of panobinostat resistance in ALL. Mechanistically, ectopic SIRT1 expression activated mitochondrial activity and sensitized ALL to panobinostat through activating mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway. Meanwhile, the transcription level of SIRT1 was significantly associated with panobinostat sensitivity across diverse tumor types and thus could be a potential biomarker of panobinostat response in cancers. Our data suggest that patients with higher SIRT1 expression in cancer cells might benefit from panobinostat treatment, supporting the implementation of combinatorial therapy with SIRT1 or mitochondrial activators to overcome panobinostat resistance. Introduction Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most prevalent malignant disease in children. 1 Long-term prognosis in children with ALL has dramatically improved in recent decades, with the 5-year event-free survival rate approaching 90%. 2 The success of ALL treatment is mainly attributed to refinement of therapy based on a better understanding of clinical and biological characteristics of the disease. However, small subsets of patients who experienced drug resistance would relapse with a dismal prognosis, and thus novel treatment strategies are needed. 3 Advances in high-throughput multi-omics have further provided insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms of ALL and drug resistance. Growing evidence has shown that many genetic and epigenetic factors are associated with drug response and ALL relapse. 4,5 In recent years, novel epigenetic modulation agents (eg, azacytidine, decitabine, and vorinostat) are promising in clinical efficacy. 6-10 For example, DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (eg, 5-azacitidine), which can remove promoter hypermethylation in tumor cells and restore the gene expression signature, have achieved significant progress in the treatment of myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome. 6,7 Furthermore, histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors such as vorinostat and panobinostat have been approved in clinical use for the treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma. 9-11 HDACs regulate chromatin structure and function by removing acetyl residues from the core histones. 5 Deregulation of HDAC activity has been closely implicated in the silencing of differentiation and tumor suppressor genes, resulting in the promotion of oncogenesis, particularly leukemia. 12,13 Interestingly, targeting HADCs has demonstrated potent antitumor activity in preclinical models and promising clinical efficacy in patients with cancer (eg, multiple myeloma and T-cell lymphoma). 14,15 Panobinostat is a pan-HDAC inhibitor and has exerted promising cytotoxic activities against different cancer cells, including ALL. 16-19 Garrido Castro et al 18 demonstrated that panobinostat exerted antileukemia activity in a B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) xenograft mouse model. Meanwhile, many clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate its therapeutic value against ALL. 20,21 Although panobinostat is a promising antileukemia agent, the efforts to maximize its clinical benefit for acute leukemia will not succeed unless more details are known about its subtype specificity, functional mechanisms, and resistance mechanisms. In the present study, we performed a genome-wide Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas)9 (CRISPR/Cas9) loss-of-function screening in B-ALL cells in the presence or absence of panobinostat to discover the molecule mechanism of its action and resistance.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study utilized genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cells, primarily Nalm6 B-ALL, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of panobinostat resistance and action. Key findings reveal mitochondrial activity as a driver of panobinostat resistance and SIRT1 expression as a critical determinant of sensitivity. Panobinostat treatment abrogates mitochondrial activity in ALL cells, contributing to resistance, while enhancing mitochondrial function (via rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression) sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat by activating the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. The investigation identifies the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway as central to panobinostat response and suggests that higher SIRT1 expression or mitochondrial hyperactivity could indicate patient benefit from panobinostat therapy. The study also details various methods used, including cell culture, gene modulation techniques, drug sensitivity assays, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and flow cytometry.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study primarily investigated Panobinostat, a pan-histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, often in combination with genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening or SIRT1 modulation. Other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide, vorinostat) and conventional chemotherapeutic agents (l-asparaginase, cytarabine, 6-mecaptopurine, vincristine, dexamethasone, daunorubicin) were mentioned for comparative or contextual analysis. Rosiglitazone, a PPAR   γ activator, was used to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance panobinostat sensitivity.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for durations of 24 hours (for RNA sequencing, combination treatments) or 14 days (for CRISPR screening), leading to 60-80% cell death and significant proliferation inhibition in Nalm6 cells. Gradient concentrations were employed for drug sensitivity assays. Rosiglitazone was administered at 31.25 µM for 24 or 48 hours. Dose-response comparisons for panobinostat sensitivity were analyzed using Sanger GDSC1 IC50 data across 576 diverse cancer cell lines. No specific doses or dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for other HDAC inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutic agents.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (driver of panobinostat resistance), decreased (by panobinostat), increased (by rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression), decreased (by SIRT1 disturbance), significantly enriched (in CRISPR/Cas9 screening for resistance), enhanced/stimulated/activated (by rosiglitazone), positively enriched (by SIRT1 overexpression), negatively enriched (by SIRT1 disturbance)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identified as the driver of panobinostat resistance. Genes associated with mitochondrial activity were 'significantly decreased' under panobinostat treatment (GSEA). Rosiglitazone 'elevated ROS levels and MMP' and 'stimulated mitochondrial biogenesis and activate OXPHOS', showing a 'synergetic effect'. SIRT1 overexpression (OE) 'significantly increased the MMP' and showed 'positive enrichment' of oxidative phosphorylation genes; SIRT1 disturbance 'significantly decreased the MMP' and showed 'negative enrichment' of oxidative phosphorylation genes. Significantly enriched in thermogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and mitochondrial-related processes (P < .05) among significantly enriched and positively selected genes at day 14 during panobinostat treatment.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates panobinostat resistance; targeting it could overcome resistance. Decreased activity contributes to resistance, allowing ALL cells to escape cell death. Enhanced activity sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat. Mitochondrial-related processes contribute to panobinostat resistance. Activating mitochondrial function can enhance chemosensitivity and overcome resistance.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (sensitized ALL to panobinostat), positively selected (CRISPR/Cas9), overexpression increases mitochondrial activity, panobinostat sensitivity, apoptosis, PMAIP1, and cleaved PARP; disturbance decreases mitochondrial activity, causes panobinostat resistance, decreases apoptosis and PMAIP1; expression negatively correlated with panobinostat sensitivity; higher expression correlated with lower sensitivity
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SIRT1 expression sensitized ALL to panobinostat through activating mitochondrial activity and the mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway. Transcription level significantly associated with panobinostat sensitivity. Among top hits/positively selected genes in CRISPR/Cas9 screening. Disturbing expression conferred significant resistance to panobinostat. SIRT1 OE 'significantly increased the MMP' and showed 'positive enrichment' of OXPHOS genes; 'increased sensitivity' to panobinostat; exhibited the 'highest proportion of apoptosis'; combined with panobinostat 'increased the expression of PMAIP1' and led to 'dramatic upregulation' of PMAIP1 and Cleaved PARP. Disturbing SIRT1 'significantly decreased the MMP' and showed 'negative enrichment' of OXPHOS genes, 'resulted in panobinostat resistance', and cells exhibited the 'lowest proportion of apoptosis', with 'lowest expression of PMAIP1' and 'modest effect' on PMAIP1 by panobinostat. SIRT1 expression and panobinostat sensitivity (IC50) showed a 'significantly negative correlation (P = .02, N = 576)' and (P < .05, N = 571). Patients with MEF2D-rearrangement, ZNF-rearrangement, hyperdiploid, mixed-lineage leukemia gene rearrangement, and TCF3-PBX1 ALL showed relatively higher expression; Patients with ETV6-RUNX1 and BCR-ABL1 fusion genes showed relatively lower expression.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulates mitochondrial activity, involved in mitochondria-related apoptosis pathway, epigenetic regulation, belongs to the Class III HDAC family; deacetylates both histone and nonhistone proteins; involved in acetylation modification, NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase, involved in aging, metabolic disorders, cancer progression, oxidative stress inhibition, P53 inactivation, MYC activation, and mitochondrial biogenesis (via PGC1-1α deacetylation).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Panobinostat sensitivity in ALL and diverse tumor types; modulation of panobinostat sensitivity in ALL cells; identified through CRISPR/Cas9 screening; response to panobinostat and other HDAC inhibitors in ALL; panobinostat therapy in ALL; SIRT1 disturbing in Nalm6 cell line, association analysis across cancer cell lines, mitochondrial activity enhancement.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for panobinostat response; higher expression indicates benefit from panobinostat treatment and supports combinatorial therapy with SIRT1 or mitochondrial activators. Knockout/disturbed expression conferred significant resistance to panobinostat, suggesting its role in panobinostat sensitivity. High SIRT1 expression sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat and increases apoptosis; disturbance leads to panobinostat resistance. SIRT1 expression could be an indicator of panobinostat sensitivity across diverse cancer types. Determinant of ALL response to panobinostat, influencing panobinostat sensitivity, a potential target for sensitizing tumor cells to panobinostat therapy. Higher SIRT1 expression is associated with increased sensitivity and potential benefit from panobinostat therapy in ALL patients, particularly in subtypes like mixed-lineage leukemia-rearranged ALL.
